Hot spots, clustering, scan statistics, near-repeat tests and surfaces of crime density.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its
help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws
one. `?name` gives the arguments and the value in full.

## Knox test of near repeats

`knxnr()`: Asks whether incidents close together in space also happen close together in time more often than chance gives: the near-repeat pattern of burglary and shootings (Knox 1964; Townsley, Homel and Chaseling 2003). Every pair of incidents within the largest distance is put in a band of distance, (ds[k - 1], ds[k]], and a band of time, (dt[l - 1], dt[l]] (the first bands start at 0 and include it), and each cell's count is compared with its expectation when the times are exchangeable among the locations, which is exact: E = S_k T_l / P, with `S_k` the pairs in distance band `k`, `T_l` the pairs in time band `l` and `P = n (n - 1) / 2`. Each cell has a one-sided permutation p-value, the times shuffled among the locations `nsim` times from `seed`, and the Poisson tail `P(X >= obs)` with the expectation as its mean, the classical Knox approximation for a rare cell. Cells are tested separately: a table of many cells shows some small p-values by chance alone. A near-repeat pattern also arises when one offender commits a series; the test speaks to timing, not to its cause.

```{r knxnr}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(150, 0, 2000), y = runif(150, 0, 2000))
k <- knxnr(p, t = runif(150, 0, 365), ds = c(200, 400), dt = c(14, 28),
           nsim = 99, seed = 2)
k
```

```{r knxnr-plot}
plot(k)
```

## Kernel intensity surface of incidents

`kdsurf()`: Where incidents cluster: the intensity lambda(u) = sum_j w_j k(u - p_j) with the product normal kernel of standard deviations `h` (along x and y), in incidents per unit area, on a regular grid or at given locations. On a grid it is the surface of `MASS::kde2d()` times the number of points, with the same default bandwidth (the normal reference 1.06 min(sd, IQR / 1.34) n^(-1/5) on each axis, a quarter of `MASS::bandwidth.nrd()`). With a study rectangle `win` the edge corrections of `spatstat.explore::density.ppp()` apply: `"uniform"` divides the intensity at `u` by `e(u)`, the share of the kernel centred at `u` inside `win` (Diggle 1985), and `"diggle"` divides each point's kernel by its own share `e(p_j)` (Jones 1993). On a grid the smallest sets of cells holding each share `cover` of the surface's mass (highest density regions, Hyndman 1996) are reported with their area: half the incidents in a few per cent of the map is concentration. The bandwidth decides how sharp the surface is and should be reported with any map.

```{r kdsurf}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = c(rnorm(80, 2, 0.5), runif(40, 0, 6)),
           y = c(rnorm(80, 3, 0.5), runif(40, 0, 6)))
k <- kdsurf(p, win = c(0, 6, 0, 6), nx = 50, edge = "uniform")
k
image(k$x, k$y, k$z)
kdsurf(p, h = 0.4, at = "points")$z[1:5]
```

```{r kdsurf-plot}
plot(k)
```

## DBSCAN clusters of incidents

`dbscn()`: Density-based clusters (Ester, Kriegel, Sander and Xu 1996): a core point has at least `minpts` points within distance `eps`, itself included; core points within `eps` of each other share a cluster, and a point that is not core but lies within `eps` of a core point (a border point) joins the first cluster that reaches it, clusters being grown from the core points in input order. The rest is noise. With `border = FALSE` border points are noise too (DBSCAN*, Campello, Moulavi and Sander 2013), which makes the result independent of the order. These are the clusters of `dbscan::dbscan()`, numbered the same way.

```{r dbscn}
set.seed(1)
p <- rbind(cbind(x = rnorm(30, 0, 0.2), y = rnorm(30, 0, 0.2)),
           cbind(x = rnorm(30, 3, 0.2), y = rnorm(30, 1, 0.2)),
           cbind(x = runif(10, -2, 5), y = runif(10, -2, 3)))
d <- dbscn(p, eps = 0.3, minpts = 5)
d
table(d$cl, useNA = "ifany")
```

## Hot spots and how long they last

`hsper()`: Counts incidents in square grid cells of side `cell` (from the corner `org`) for each period and marks as hot, in each period, the `k = ceiling(top * m)` busiest of the `m` cells that ever hold an incident, with every cell tied with the k-th; when a tie would make more than 2 k cells hot the counts do not single them out and the tied cells are left out (counted in `tiedout`). Each period gets its concentration (the fewest cells holding half its incidents), the share of its incidents in hot cells, and the Jaccard overlap of its hot set with the period before (`NA` when either is empty); each cell gets the number of periods it was hot and its longest run of successive hot periods, the persistence that tells chronic hot spots from flare-ups (Weisburd, Bushway, Lum and Yang 2004).

```{r hsper}
set.seed(1)
n <- 600
p <- cbind(x = c(rnorm(300, 2, 0.3), runif(300, 0, 10)),
           y = c(rnorm(300, 2, 0.3), runif(300, 0, 10)))
h <- hsper(p, prd = rep(2021:2024, length.out = n), cell = 1, top = 0.1)
h
subset(h$cells, nhot == 4)
```

```{r hsper-plot}
plot(h)
```

## Empirical-Bayes shrinkage of hot-spot counts

`ebshr()`: The places with the highest counts in one period tend to fall in the next by chance alone: a count `y = theta + e` is a true rate plus noise of variance `v` (for Poisson counts, the mean count, the default). The linear shrinkage estimate (1 - B) y + B ybar toward the weighted mean has expected loss (1 - B)^2 S_e + B^2 S_theta when the noise has weighted mean 0 and is uncorrelated with the rates, which is smallest at B* = S_e / (S_e + S_theta), where it never exceeds the loss of the raw counts (James and Stein 1961; Efron and Morris 1975). `S_theta` is estimated as the excess of the weighted scatter of `y` over `v` (0 if negative). The predicted fall of a place is `B (y - ybar)`: the size of the regression to the mean a hot-spot programme should expect without doing anything. That B* lies in [0, 1], minimises the loss and never does worse than no shrinkage is proved in Lean: see `proof("ebshr")`.

```{r ebshr}
y <- c(40, 12, 9, 25, 7, 31, 5, 18)
s <- ebshr(y)
s
s$est[which.max(y), ]
```

```{r ebshr-plot}
plot(s)
```

## Space-time scan statistic of incidents

`kscan()`: Kulldorff's space-time permutation scan (Kulldorff, Heffernan, Hartman, Assuncao and Mostashari 2005), which needs the incidents alone, no population: cylinders are circles of radius <code>r</code> about each distinct incident location times windows [s, s + tw) that start at each distinct incident time. A cylinder holding `c` incidents, of `n_C` in its circle (at any time) and `n_W` in its window (anywhere), expects e = n_C n_W / n when place and time are independent, and scores the Poisson log-likelihood ratio c log(c / e) + (n - c) log((n - c) / (n - e)) when `c > e`, 0 otherwise (Kulldorff 1997). The most likely cluster has the largest ratio; secondary clusters follow in order of their ratio, each the best of its circle among those whose circles overlap none chosen before. Each p-value compares the cluster's ratio with the largest ratio of the whole scan with the times shuffled among the locations `nsim` times from `seed`, so a secondary cluster's p-value is conservative. The shuffles run over the incidents in the order of their coordinates and times, so the clusters and the p-values do not depend on the order of the rows; a tie in the ratio goes to the centre first in that order. That the ratio is never negative is proved in Lean: see `proof("kscan")`. The work grows as the number of locations times `length(r)` times the distinct times times `length(tw)`, for the scan and for each permutation.

```{r kscan}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = c(runif(150, 0, 20), rnorm(20, 5, 0.3)),
           y = c(runif(150, 0, 20), rnorm(20, 15, 0.3)))
t <- c(sample(0:99, 150, TRUE), sample(40:44, 20, TRUE))
s <- kscan(p, t = t, r = c(1, 3), tw = c(5, 20), top = 2, nsim = 99,
           seed = 1)
s
```

```{r kscan-plot}
plot(s)
```

## Global Moran's I with its inference

`gmoran()`: Moran's (1950) I of values on units with spatial weights `w`: with `z = x - mean(x)`, I = n / S0 sum_ij w_ij z_i z_j / sum z_i^2, its expectation `-1 / (n - 1)` and its variance under normality and under randomisation (Cliff and Ord 1981), the z statistics and their upper normal tails (positive autocorrelation: neighbours alike), and, with `nsim > 0`, the permutation p-value (1 + #{I* >= I}) / (nsim + 1), the values shuffled over the units from `seed`. These are the statistics of `spdep::moran.test()` and `spdep::moran.mc()`. Given a matrix or data frame, each column is tested on the same weights: one row per category or year, a sweep of a variable across a polygon surface. `lmorn()` gives the local statistics, which add up to S0 I with row-standardised weights.

```{r gmoran}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(50), y = runif(50))
w <- spwt(p, k = 4)
gmoran(p[, 1] + rnorm(50, sd = 0.2), w, nsim = 99, seed = 1)
# a sweep over three yearly counts
gmoran(data.frame(y1 = rpois(50, 3), y2 = rpois(50, 3 + 4 * p[, 1]),
                  y3 = rpois(50, 9 * p[, 1])), w)
```

## Bivariate Moran's I

`bvmor()`: Whether high values of one variable sit next to high values of another (Wartenberg 1985): with `zx` and `zy` the centred values, I = n / S0 sum_ij w_ij zx_i zy_j / sqrt(sum zx^2 sum zy^2), which is Moran's I (`gmoran()`) when `y` is `x` (proved in Lean: see `proof("bvmor")`) and, with row-standardised weights, `spdep::moran_bv()`'s statistic. Inference is by permutation: `y`'s values are shuffled over the units `nsim` times from `seed` while `x` stays, so under the null its expectation is 0. The statistic mixes the two variables' correlation at a unit with their spatial association; it is not a test of spillover from `x` to `y`.

```{r bvmor}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60), y = runif(60))
a <- p[, 1] + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3)
b <- p[, 1] + rnorm(60, sd = 0.3)
bvmor(a, b, spwt(p, k = 5), nsim = 199, seed = 1)
```

## Spatial regression: lag, error and combined models

`sarml()`: Fits the spatial lag model y = rho W y + X beta + e, the spatial error model y = X beta + u with u = lambda W u + e, or both at once (`"sac"`, one weights matrix for both), with normal errors, by maximum likelihood (Ord 1975; Anselin 1988): the likelihood is concentrated in `rho` or `lambda` and maximised by Brent's method on (-1 / m, 1 / m), `m` the largest row sum of `W` (which bounds its spectral radius), with log |I - rho W| from a dense LU factorisation, so the cost grows as `n^3` per evaluation (at most 5000 units). The combined model is maximised over both parameters by Nelder and Mead's simplex. Standard errors come from the inverse of the expected information matrix (Anselin 1988, ch. 6); these are the estimates of `spatialreg::lagsarlm()`, `errorsarlm()` and `sacsarlm()`. `durbin = TRUE` adds the lags W x of the varying columns (the spatial Durbin model, or the Durbin error model). `method = "2sls"` fits the lag model by two-stage least squares with the instruments W x and W^2 x (Kelejian and Prucha 1998), as `spatialreg::stsls()` does, without a likelihood; its standard errors divide the residual sum of squares by `n` less the coefficients.

```{r sarml}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(80), y = runif(80))
w <- spwt(p, k = 5)
W <- matrix(0, 80, 80)
W[cbind(w$i, w$j)] <- w$w
x <- rnorm(80)
y <- solve(diag(80) - 0.5 * W, 1 + 2 * x + rnorm(80))
f <- sarml(y, x, w)
f
spill(f)
```

```{r sarml-plot}
plot(f)
```

## Direct, indirect and total effects of a spatial lag model

`spill()`: In a model with a spatial lag of the outcome, y = rho W y + X beta + W X theta + e, a change in covariate `k` at every unit moves the outcomes by S_k = (I - rho W)^-1 (beta_k I + theta_k W): the mean of its diagonal is the direct effect, the mean row sum the total, and their difference the indirect effect, the spillover to other units (LeSage and Pace 2009). An analysis that reads `beta_k` alone can report "no effect" where the effect is all spillover. With row-standardised weights the total is `(beta_k + theta_k) / (1 - rho)`, proved in Lean: see `proof("spill")`. Standard errors are by the delta method in `rho`, `beta_k` and `theta_k`, with the exact derivatives d (I - rho W)^-1 / d rho = (I - rho W)^-1 W (I - rho W)^-1. The effects are those of `spatialreg::impacts()`, which gives simulated rather than delta-method standard errors.

```{r spill}
set.seed(2)
p <- cbind(x = runif(40), y = runif(40))
w <- spwt(p, k = 4)
spill(w = w, rho = 0.4, b = c(gent = 0.1), th = 0.3)
```

## Cross-type K function and the segregation test

`crossk()`: Whether incidents of one type (`i`) have incidents of another (`j`) near them more than independence gives: the cross-type K function K_ij(r) = A / (n_i n_j) sum e_ab 1(d_ab <= r) over pairs of a point `a` of type `i` and a point `b` of type `j` in the rectangle `win` of area `A`, with Ripley's (1977) isotropic correction `e_ab` (the length of the circle about `a` through `b` over its length inside `win`), and `L = sqrt(K / pi)` (Lotwick and Silverman 1982). Under independence K = pi r^2. With `i` equal to `j` it is Ripley's K of that type. These are the values of `spatstat.explore::Kcross()` with `correction = "isotropic"`.

```{r crossk}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(120), y = runif(120))
m <- ifelse(p[, 1] < 0.5, "burglary", "robbery")
crossk(p, marks = m, i = "burglary", j = "robbery",
       win = c(0, 1, 0, 1), r = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), sigma = 0.1,
       nsim = 19, seed = 1)
```

## Quadrat count test

`qdrtst()`: Counts the points in an `nx` by `ny` grid of equal tiles of the rectangle `win` and tests complete spatial randomness by Pearson's chi-square, `X2 = sum (n_k - e)^2 / e` with `e` the mean count, on nx ny - 1 degrees of freedom: the upper tail against clustering and the two-sided p-value (twice the smaller tail, `quadrat.test()`'s default), which also flags regular patterns. A point on an inner tile boundary goes to the tile above or to its right, one on the outer edge to the tile inside. These are the values of `spatstat.explore::quadrat.test()`. The counts feed `morsta()`.

```{r qdrtst}
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(100, 0, 2), y = runif(100))
q <- qdrtst(p, win = c(0, 2, 0, 1), nx = 4, ny = 2)
q
morsta(q$counts)
```

```{r qdrtst-plot}
plot(q)
```

## Morisita's index of dispersion

`morsta()`: Morisita's (1959) index of the counts in `n` equal quadrats, I = n (sum x^2 - S) / (S^2 - S) with `S` the total: 1 for a random pattern, above for clumping (`n` when all fall in one quadrat), below for an even spread. The uniform and clumped indices are the values of `I` at the `crit / 2` tails of chi-square on `n - 1` degrees of freedom, and the standardised index of Smith-Gill (1975) maps `I` onto [-1, 1] with them at `-0.5` and `0.5`; `chi = I (S - 1) + n - S` has the chi-square distribution under randomness. These are the values of `vegan::dispindmorisita()`.

```{r morsta}
morsta(c(3, 0, 7, 12, 1, 4, 0, 9))
```

## Indices of residential segregation

`dissix()`: The evenness of groups across areal units (Massey and Denton 1988), from a table of counts with one row per unit and one column per group: Duncan's dissimilarity D = sum |x_ik / X_k - x_il / X_l| / 2 between each pair of groups (the share of either group that would have to move for the two to be spread alike), and for each group against the rest the segregation index `IS`, Theil's entropy index `H`, Atkinson's index with shape `delta` and the Gini index. With weights `w` between the units, Morrill's (1991) adjusted `D` subtracts the weighted mean absolute difference of the pair's shares between neighbouring units, so that segregation across a boundary counts less than segregation within. Units with no one in them are left out. That `D` lies between 0 and 1 is proved in Lean: see `proof("dissix")`.

```{r dissix}
x <- cbind(a = c(90, 80, 10, 5, 50), b = c(10, 20, 85, 95, 50))
dissix(x)
dissix(x, w = spwt(nb = list(2, c(1, 3), c(2, 4), c(3, 5), 4),
                   type = "contig"))$dm
```

## Points in polygons, and the population the units cover

`pinpl()`: Finds the region holding each point (a facility, a station, an incident) by the even-odd rule, a point on a boundary counting as inside; a region given as several rings (parts and holes) is one region, and a hole is any ring inside another of the same region. A point outside every region gets `NA`; one inside overlapping regions takes the first by label and `nreg` says how many hold it. Coordinates are taken as planar (longitude and latitude work for regions small enough that their edges are straight in degrees).

```{r pinpl}
sq <- function(x0, id) {
  data.frame(x = x0 + c(0, 1, 1, 0), y = c(0, 0, 1, 1), id = id)
}
poly <- rbind(sq(0, "A"), sq(1, "B"), sq(2, "C"))
u <- pinpl(cbind(x = c(0.5, 0.2, 2.5, 9), y = c(0.5, 0.7, 0.5, 9)),
           poly = poly, pop = c(1200, 800, 450))
u
u$reg
```

```{r pinpl-plot}
plot(u)
```

## Crosswalk of counts between two sets of areal units

`arwt()`: Moves values (counts, populations) kept on one set of units (an old boundary version, say) onto another, through the pairs of a source and a target unit that overlap: each source's value is split among its targets in proportion to `area`, the size of the overlap (its area, or its population for a population-weighted crosswalk), which assumes the value spread uniformly over the source. Where each source lies in one target (a boundary version that only merges units) the result is exact aggregation and `exact` is `TRUE`; splitting a source is an approximation. A source with no pair is lost (`lost`), and each source's main target (its largest share) maps an old identifier onto the new scheme. The concentration of the result across the targets is reported as the Gini coefficient and the share of the largest `top` targets.

```{r arwt}
# four old units onto three new ones; unit d is split 70/30 by area
arwt(c(a = 120, b = 40, c = 60, d = 100),
     from = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "d"), to = c("N1", "N1", "N2", "N2", "N3"),
     area = c(1, 1, 1, 7, 3), top = 1)
```

## Crosswalk between boundary versions

`bndxw()`: Carries values kept on one set of areas (the 158 neighbourhoods of a city's new boundaries, a census vintage's tracts) to another (the 140 old neighbourhoods) through a correspondence table: each link says what share `w` of a source area's value falls in a target area. Counts of a source wholly inside one target move whole (weight 1, exact); a source split between targets is shared by area or population (uniform density within the source, an assumption). The same table read the other way disaggregates. `map` also gives each source's main target, the column to add to a table keyed by the source areas.

```{r bndxw}
# old areas a, b merge into A; c splits between A and B by area
bndxw(from = c("a", "b", "c", "c"), to = c("A", "A", "A", "B"),
      x = c(3, 4, 5, 8), unit = c("a", "b", "b", "c"),
      w = c(1, 1, 0.25, 0.75))
```

## Synthetic exposure of areas from a survey

`synexp()`: A small-area synthetic estimate (Gonzalez and Hoza 1978): the prevalence of a trait (serious mental illness, say, for the benchmark of a disparity in police use of force) is modelled on survey microdata by logistic regression (`lgtreg()`); applied to each area's covariates it gives the area's rate, and times its population the number of people with the trait, the exposure a rate per person needs. The area covariates must be on the scale of the survey's (shares of an area for indicators read as the probability of the indicator, a plug-in that assumes the model holds within areas).

```{r synexp}
set.seed(1)
s <- data.frame(age = runif(400, 18, 80), male = rbinom(400, 1, 0.5))
y <- rbinom(400, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.02 * s$age + 0.4 * s$male))
areas <- data.frame(age = c(35, 52), male = c(0.48, 0.51))
synexp(y, s, areas, pop = c(12000, 8000))$areas
```

## Treated, comparison and excluded places around sites

`bufas()`: The buffer design of place-based evaluations: a place (a block, an address) within distance <code>r</code> of a site (a new facility, a treated corner) is treated; one within <code>r</code> of a comparison point and farther than `buf` from every site is a comparison; the rest are excluded, so that spillover from the sites (displacement or a diffusion of benefits, Bowers and Johnson 2003) does not reach the comparison. `buf` should be several times <code>r</code>.

```{r bufas}
set.seed(4)
p <- cbind(x = runif(200, 0, 5000), y = runif(200, 0, 5000))
b <- bufas(p, site = cbind(c(1000, 3500), c(1200, 3000)),
           comp = cbind(c(2500, 4500), c(500, 4000)), r = 330)
b
```

```{r bufas-plot}
plot(b)
```

## Weighted displacement quotient: did crime move next door?

`wdqx()`: Asks whether an intervention in an area pushed crime into the area around it (displacement) or reduced it there too (a diffusion of benefits). Counts before and after the intervention are needed for the treated area `a`, a buffer `b` around it and a control area `c` that neither can reach (see `bufas()` for drawing them). With subscripts 0 before and 1 after, the measures of Bowers and Johnson (2003), as Guerette (2009, Appendix B, equations 1 to 4) states them:

```{r wdqx}
# burglaries: treated 100 -> 60, buffer 50 -> 40, control 200 -> 180
wdqx(a = c(100, 60), b = c(50, 40), c = c(200, 180))
# Guerette (2009), Appendix D
wdqx(a = c(207, 110), b = c(178, 157), c = c(308, 318))
```

## Prospective hot-spotting: where the next burglaries are likely

`prohs()`: Asks which places are at most risk in the coming days, given where and when crimes happened recently. Burglary risk is raised near a recent burglary for a few weeks (the near-repeat pattern), so Bowers, Johnson and Pease (2004) score each cell of a grid by the recent incidents near it, each weighted down with its distance and its age:

```{r prohs}
set.seed(6)
n <- 300
p <- cbind(x = runif(n, 0, 2000), y = runif(n, 0, 2000))
day <- sort(sample(1:120, n, TRUE))
r <- prohs(p, t = day, at = 100, win = c(0, 2000, 0, 2000), cell = 100,
           bw = 400, ahead = 14)
r$eval
image(r$x, r$y, r$z)
```

```{r prohs-plot}
plot(r)
```

## Crime linkage: which crimes belong to one series

`lnkpr()`: Asks whether two crimes were committed by the same offender, from how far apart they are in space and time and how alike the offender behaved (the modus operandi: entry method, property taken, a weapon shown). For every pair of crimes it gives the distance, the time between them and the Jaccard similarity of their behaviours (the behaviours present in both over those present in either; 0 when neither shows any). On the pairs of solved crimes, linked when they belong to the same series, a logistic regression of being linked on the three measures is fitted and each measure's power to tell linked from unlinked pairs is the area under its ROC curve (AUC: the chance that a linked pair is closer, sooner or more alike than an unlinked one; 0.5 is no better than chance), as Bennell and Canter (2002) did for commercial burglaries. The fitted model then scores every pair, including those with an unsolved crime: `prob` is the estimated chance that the two are linked.

```{r lnkpr}
set.seed(9)
s <- rep(1:6, each = 5)
cx <- runif(6, 0, 5000)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 1500)
cy <- runif(6, 0, 5000)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 1500)
day <- runif(6, 0, 300)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 60)
mo <- matrix(rbinom(30 * 5, 1, 0.3), 30)
sr <- ifelse(runif(30) < 0.2, NA, s)
r <- lnkpr(cbind(x = cx, y = cy), t = day, series = sr, mo = mo)
r$coef
r$auc
```

```{r lnkpr-plot}
plot(r)
```

## Accuracy of a hot-spot map

`hsacc()`: Asks how well a map of predicted hot spots (from `kdsurf()`, `prohs()`, `rtmfit()` or any score per cell) caught the crimes that followed. The hot cells are those of highest predicted score whose areas together first reach the share `top` of the study area (or the cells marked `TRUE` when `pred` is logical). Then:

```{r hsacc}
set.seed(12)
risk <- rgamma(400, 0.5)
before <- rpois(400, risk)
after <- rpois(400, risk)
hsacc(pred = before, obs = after, top = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2), prev = before)
```

## Risk terrain model

`rtmfit()`: Risk terrain modelling (Caplan, Kennedy and Miller 2011) relates the crimes counted in the cells of a grid to risk layers, the presence or density of features (bars, transit stops, vacant lots) around each cell, by Poisson regression. The exponentiated coefficient of a layer is its relative risk value; the cells' relative risk combines the layers.

```{r rtmfit}
rtmfit(c(1, 2, 4, 8, 3, 5), list(bars = c(0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1),
                                 stops = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0)))
# layers from feature locations
cell <- as.matrix(expand.grid(x = 1:4, y = 1:4))
bars <- rbind(c(1, 1), c(3, 4))
y <- c(3, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3)
rtmfit(y, list(bars = bars), cell = cell, rad = 1.5, kind = "dens")$coef
```

## Choropleth maps in base graphics

`chomap()`: `chomap()` shades each area of a map by the class of its value, with no spatial package: an area is a matrix of coordinates. The class breaks, the class of each value and the bounding box are computed by the compiled kernel; R only draws. Areas are drawn with `polypath()`, so a ring inside another is a hole.

```{r chomap}
sq <- function(x0, y0) cbind(x0 + c(0, 1, 1, 0), y0 + c(0, 0, 1, 1))
p <- list(a = sq(0, 0), b = sq(1, 0), c = sq(0, 1), d = sq(1, 1))
chomap(p, c(12, 3, 7, 25), brk = 2)
chomap(p, c(12, 3, 7, 25), brk = c(0, 5, 10, 30), main = "Rates")
```

## Small multiples of a choropleth map by period

`smmap()`: `smmap()` draws one choropleth map per period in a grid of panels, all with the same class breaks and colours, so that a change between periods is a change of shade. The areas, breaks and classes are those of `chomap()`, the breaks computed from the values of every period together; the legend is drawn in the last panel.

```{r smmap}
sq <- function(x0, y0) cbind(x0 + c(0, 1, 1, 0), y0 + c(0, 0, 1, 1))
p <- list(sq(0, 0), sq(1, 0), sq(0, 1), sq(1, 1))
v <- cbind(`2022` = c(3, 8, 5, 1), `2023` = c(4, 9, 2, 1),
           `2024` = c(6, 12, 2, 0))
smmap(p, v, brk = 3)
```

## Point maps, with clusters

`ptmap()`: `ptmap()` draws points on a map at an aspect of 1, optionally coloured by cluster: a result of `dbscn()` or a cluster number per point. Each cluster has its own colour and point shape (so the clusters read in grey print too) and its number at its centre, the mean of its points; noise is drawn as grey crosses. The box and the cluster centres are computed by the compiled kernel; R only draws. `plot()` of a `dbscn()` result draws it through `ptmap()`, given the points it was found in.

```{r ptmap}
set.seed(1)
p <- rbind(cbind(rnorm(30, 0, 0.2), rnorm(30, 0, 0.2)),
           cbind(rnorm(30, 3, 0.2), rnorm(30, 1, 0.2)),
           cbind(runif(10, -2, 5), runif(10, -2, 3)))
ptmap(p)
d <- dbscn(p, eps = 0.3, minpts = 5)
plot(d, p)
```

## Proportional symbol maps

`prpmap()`: `prpmap()` draws a circle at each point (a district's centre, say) whose area is proportional to its value: the radius is `rmax` times the square root of the value over the largest value, so the largest has radius `rmax`. The circles are drawn largest first, so that the smaller stay visible over them, and filled half-transparent. The radii, the drawing order and the box (widened by `rmax` on every side so the circles fit) are computed by the compiled kernel; R only draws.

```{r prpmap}
x <- c(0, 4, 1, 3, 2)
y <- c(0, 1, 3, 4, 2)
prpmap(x, y, c(120, 30, 5, 60, 0))
prpmap(cbind(x, y), v = c(120, 30, NA, 60, 10), rmax = 1)
```

## Empirical orthogonal functions of a space-time matrix

`eofst()`: `eofst()` decomposes a matrix of counts or rates, one row per period and one column per place, into empirical orthogonal functions (EOFs): spatial patterns (the columns of `eofs`) whose weights over time (the principal component series, the columns of `pcs`) reproduce the centred matrix, ordered by the share of its variance each explains. A leading pattern that loads on a cluster of places, with a series that rises, is a hot spot that grows; a second pattern of opposite signs is a shift of crime from one set of places to another.

```{r eofst}
set.seed(3)
yr <- 1:10
z <- outer(yr, c(1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)) + matrix(rnorm(60), 10)
colnames(z) <- paste0("ward", 1:6)
e <- eofst(z)
e
round(e$eofs[, 1], 2)
```

## Thin-plate spline surface

`tpsurf()`: `tpsurf()` fits a thin-plate spline to values measured at points in the plane (rates at area centroids, say) and evaluates it on a grid over their box: a smooth surface that passes through the values when `lam` is 0 and is smoothed towards a plane as `lam` grows. It complements `kdsurf()`, which smooths the points themselves rather than values at them.

```{r tpsurf}
set.seed(2)
x <- runif(40)
y <- runif(40)
s <- tpsurf(x, y, sin(4 * x) + y^2 + rnorm(40, sd = 0.05), lam = 0.001,
            nx = 30)
s
plot(s)
```

```{r tpsurf-plot}
plot(s)
```
